title: The jewel discourse
hookLine: a city in crisis, and a verse chanted along its walls through the night

cards: Vesali was a rich city, run by a council of nobles called the Licchavis. And then, the story goes, everything went wrong at once. The rains failed.
Crops died. People starved, and sickness spread through the streets, and the city was full of dread. The council sent messengers south to Rajagaha to ask the Buddha to come.
He came. And the tradition says that the moment he set foot in their territory, the sky opened and it poured. Then he gave Ananda a set of verses to carry through the city.

teach.h: ANANDA WALKS THE WALLS AT NIGHT
teach.b: The poem is the Ratana Sutta, the discourse on the jewel.
The story around it comes from the commentary: Ananda walked along the city walls all night, chanting the verses and sprinkling water from the Buddha's bowl, and the city recovered.

teach.h: MAY ALL BEINGS HERE BE HAPPY
teach.b: The poem itself starts by speaking to every being gathered there, visible or not: may all of you be happy, and listen. Show kindness to the humans who bring you offerings day and night, and protect them.
Then come the verses that give it its name. Whatever treasure there is in this world or any other, nothing equals the one who has fully awakened. Then a line that ends verse after verse, like a bell.
In Pali: etena saccena suvatthi hotu.

teach.h: BY THIS TRUTH, MAY THERE BE WELL-BEING
teach.b: By this truth, may there be well-being. It's called an act of truth. Behind it is an old Indian idea: that stating something deeply true, solemnly, has power.

So the poem states truths: the Buddha is a jewel, the teaching is a jewel, the community of noble disciples is a jewel. And on each truth, it rests a wish for safety. One verse near the end holds a quiet image.

teach.h: THE WISE GO OUT LIKE THIS LAMP
teach.b: The old is used up, nothing new arises; the wise go out, the poem says, like this lamp.
Picture Ananda saying that at night, perhaps holding a flame. Theravada monks still chant this poem when a home is blessed and when someone is sick.

how: The Ratana Sutta is one of the paritta, or protective texts, of Theravada Buddhism; monks chant it at blessings, for the sick, and in times of public crisis, often over a bowl of water that is then sprinkled.

s: the story of Vesali's crisis comes from the commentary, not the poem itself
the verses themselves don't name the city; the story around them is the commentary's.
the poem's refrain is a wish for well-being resting on a truth
by this truth, may there be well-being.
the Ratana Sutta is no longer chanted today
monks across Theravada countries still chant it at blessings, for the sick and in crises.

games.q: you're Ananda. the city is sick and frightened, and the Buddha has given you verses. what do you do, the story says?
o: read them once in the market and leave.
walk the city walls all night, chanting and sprinkling water.
keep them for the monks only.
games.why: the commentary says Ananda went around the walls through the night, chanting and sprinkling water from the Buddha's bowl.

practice: Think of a person or a place that needs safety right now.

If you chant, say the Pali refrain slowly, three times, etena saccena suvatthi hotu; if you'd rather, just hold its meaning, by this truth, may there be well-being, and let the words rest there like water sprinkled gently.

wordCard.voice: Ratana, jewel. The Ratana Sutta: truths about the Buddha, the teaching and the community, each one ending with a wish for well-being, chanted in times of fear. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali ratana (Sanskrit ratna): jewel, treasure. the three jewels are the Buddha, the teaching and the community.

carryVoice: Your line: the jewel. A true thing, said gently for someone else's safety. Until tomorrow.
